Workout Splits: Find the Right Training Split for You

A workout split is how you divide your training across the week. Compare the main options, see which fit your schedule, and take your pick straight into the planner.

Find My Split → Build a Workout

What is a workout split?

A workout split (also called a training split or gym split) is the plan that decides which muscles you train on which days. Instead of training everything every session, you divide the work — by body region, by movement type, or not at all — so that each session is manageable and each muscle gets time to recover before it is trained again.

Choosing a split is really choosing three things at once: how often you train each muscle, how much you do per session, and how many days you need to commit. There is no universally best option, only the best fit for your schedule, goals and recovery.

Compare the main workout splits

SplitDays / weekMuscle frequencySessionLevelBest for
PPL 6 2× (6-day) / 1× (3-day) 60–75 min Intermediate Intermediates who want high volume and can train 5–6 days
Bro Split 5 1× 45–60 min Intermediate Lifters who enjoy dedicated muscle days and 5 sessions a week
Upper/Lower 4 2× 55–70 min Beginner Most lifters on 4 days; strength and size together
Full Body 3 2–3× 45–60 min Beginner Beginners and anyone training 2–3 days a week
Arnold Split 6 2× 75–90 min Advanced Advanced lifters chasing high-volume, high-frequency training
PPLUL 5 2× (most muscles) 60–75 min Intermediate Intermediates who want near-twice-weekly frequency on five days

Frequency shows how often each muscle is trained per week in the standard version of the split.

How to choose the right split

  1. Start with days per week. Pick a number you can keep up for months, not the number you can manage this week.
  2. Match your experience. Beginners tend to progress well on full body or upper/lower; PPL and Arnold work best once you have a training base.
  3. Consider session length. Full body means fewer, longer sessions; body-part splits mean shorter, more frequent ones.
  4. Think about recovery. More days means less time between sessions. Sleep, food and stress matter as much as the split itself.
  5. Check your equipment. Most splits adapt to dumbbells and bodyweight, but body-part days lean on machines and cables.

Frequently asked questions

How many days a week should I train?

Three to four days suits most people. Two days works for a busy schedule and five or six only makes sense if you recover well and want more volume.

How often should I train each muscle?

Training each muscle about twice a week is a practical middle ground and easy to organise, but once or three times a week can also work if total weekly volume is sensible.

Is it OK to change my split?

Yes. Many lifters change split as their schedule, goals or experience change. Give a plan at least 8–12 weeks before judging it.
